authors: Hansford HJ, Berg B, Grotle M, Austevoll IM, Dahabreh IJ, Hellum C, Ingebrigtsen T, Jones MD, Lee H, Solberg TK, Storheim K, McAuley JH, Cashin AG.
summary:
Background

Randomized trials have shown limited benefits and increased risks of adding spinal fusion surgery to decompression for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Decompression with fusion has increasingly been used in the United States.

Objective

To examine the comparative effectiveness of decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for patient subgroups.

Design

Cohort study using the target trial framework.

Setting

Norwegian Registry for Spine Surgery and nested NORDSTEN-DS (Norwegian degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis) randomized trial.

Patients

Adults aged 18 to 80 years with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least 3 months.

Intervention

Lumbar spinal decompression surgery with fusion versus lumbar spinal decompression surgery alone.

Measurements

The primary outcomes were Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score and reoperation at 12 months. Linear regression models with inverse probability weighting to control for baseline confounding were used to obtain effect estimates with 95% CIs for decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age, smoking, body mass index (BMI), back pain intensity, and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade.

Results

Of 2252 patients, 236 were in the NORDSTEN-DS randomized trial. The mean age was 66 years, and 1576 (70%) women were included. A total of 1446 patients had decompression alone, and 806 had decompression with fusion; respective unadjusted baseline ODI scores were 38.9 (SD, 14.9) and 41.4 (SD, 14.7). At 12 months, the ODI score was 22.3 (95% CI, 15.5 to 29.1) for decompression alone and 20.0 (CI, 13.9 to 26.2) for decompression with fusion; the mean difference was 2.2 (CI, -1.6 to 6.1). In exploratory analyses, the ODI score was worse for decompression with fusion for men with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. Reoperation risk at 12 months did not differ.

Limitation

Possible residual confounding.

Conclusion

Patient subgroups did not have differential effects from the addition of fusion to decompression at 12 months.

Primary funding source

Research Council of Norway.
title: Decompression With or Without Fusion Across Subgroups With Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis : A Target Trial Emulation.

summary:
Background

Long COVID (LC) is widespread; however, limited information has been reported on the likelihood that symptoms remit over time.

Objective

To evaluate the likelihood of improvement among persons with likely LC.

Design

Prospective, multisite cohort study (RECOVER-Adult [Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery]).

Setting

83 U.S.-based sites across 33 states; Washington, DC; and Puerto Rico.

Participants

1019 persons in RECOVER-Adult with likely LC (LC Research Index [LCRI] ≥11) 12 months after first SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Measurements

The primary outcome was time until 2 consecutive study visits with LCRI less than 11. Secondary outcomes were time until LCRI measure reduced 50% or more and quality of life was good or better, and LCRI decreased to 0. Unadjusted estimates of cumulative incidence and adjusted marginal cumulative incidence by age, sex, SARS-CoV-2 wave, and LC subtype were reported across all follow-up time points.

Results

An estimated 36.2% (95% CI, 33.0% to 39.5%) met the primary outcome by 24 months after infection, and 50.1% (CI, 46.1% to 54.0%) met the primary outcome by 36 months. An estimated 56.4% (CI, 52.2% to 60.4%) and 26.9% (CI, 23.3% to 30.5%), respectively, met the 2 secondary outcomes by 36 months. Among persons who still reported likely LC at 18 months and 24 months after first infection, relative timing of subsequent symptom improvement was similar.

Limitation

Findings in this observational cohort are interpretable in a population with prevalent likely LC and do not address causal relationships between individual characteristics and symptom improvement.

Conclusion

Among persons with likely LC 12 months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, one half experience meaningful reductions in symptoms by 36 months, whereas a quarter experience complete remission of symptoms. These findings underscore both the potential for natural recovery and the urgent need for placebo-controlled therapeutic intervention trials.

Primary funding source

National Institutes of Health.
title: Timing of Long COVID Improvement in Prospectively Followed RECOVER-Adult Participants.

authors: Olij B, Pilz da Cunha G, Pugh SA, Abu Hilal M, Lopez-Lopez V, Aghayan D, Brusadin R, Fichtinger RS, Ratti F, Kuemmerli C, Sijberden JP, Besselink MG, Troisi RI, Brandts L, Primrose JN, Edwin B, Robles-Campos R, van Dam RM, Fretland ÅA, LLR vs OLR IPDMA Collaborators.
summary:
Background

Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have compared laparoscopic liver resection (LLR) and open liver resection (OLR) for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM); however, long-term outcomes and subgroup effects have not been comprehensively evaluated.

Purpose

To compare postoperative and long-term oncologic outcomes after LLR versus OLR for CRLM using individual participant data from RCTs.

Data sources

PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception through March 2025 for RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.

Study selection

Eligible studies were RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.

Data extraction

Individual participant data, including unpublished data, were obtained from trial investigators of all 4 published RCTs.

Data synthesis

Analyses used a modified intention-to-treat approach and 1-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA) with trial-adjusted regression models and g-computation to estimate standardized treatment effects across outcomes, with 95% CIs obtained by nonparametric bootstrap resampling. Prespecified subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity of treatment effect for the primary outcome. A total of 761 patients were included (laparoscopic, n = 384; open, n = 377). Postoperative morbidity was lower in patients assigned to laparoscopic surgery compared with open surgery (19% vs. 27%). Among patients who received preoperative systemic therapy, morbidity did not differ between groups (25% vs. 24%). Ninety-day mortality was 1.8% after LLR and 0.8% after OLR. After a median follow-up of 93 months, overall survival and disease-free survival did not differ between groups.

Limitation

Analyses were limited to variables available across all studies.

Conclusion

In this IPDMA of all published RCTs in the field, LLR for CRLM was associated with lower postoperative morbidity than OLR, with similar long-term oncologic outcomes.

Primary funding source

None. (PROSPERO: CRD42024502655).
title: Laparoscopic Versus Open Liver Resection for Colorectal Liver Metastases : An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Four Randomized Clinical Trials.

authors: Yun JS, Mun H, Jung JH, Park Y, Kim SY, Kim K, Ko SH, Ahn YB, Kwon HS, Han K, Son JW.
summary:
Background

Obesity and early-onset cancer are both increasing among young adults, yet evidence remains limited.

Objective

To assess associations between obesity and early-onset cancer risk in young adults.

Design

Nationwide population-based cohort study.

Setting

Korean National Health Insurance Service database, 2009 to 2021.

Patients

6 313 338 adults aged 20 to 39 years without prior cancer, from a national health screening program.

Measurements

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into 5 groups (underweight to class II obesity) according to Asian-specific criteria. The outcome was incident cancer.

Results

During a mean follow-up of 11.2 years, 151 893 cancer cases occurred. Ten-year cumulative incidence ranged from 1.84% (95% CI, 1.83% to 1.86%) in the normal-weight group to 2.24% (CI, 2.22% to 2.27%) in class I obesity and 2.62% (CI, 2.56% to 2.68%) in class II obesity, with absolute risk differences of 0.40% (CI, 0.39% to 0.41%) and 0.78% (CI, 0.73% to 0.82%). The relative association was more pronounced in men, and absolute risk differences were greater in women. In combined BMI-waist circumference analyses, people with class I obesity based on BMI and with abdominal obesity had higher 10-year cumulative incidence (2.45% [CI, 2.41% to 2.50%]) than those without abdominal obesity (2.13% [CI, 2.10% to 2.16%]), exceeding that of those with class II obesity without abdominal obesity (2.20% [CI, 2.03% to 2.36%]). The highest cumulative incidence was observed for thyroid, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Obesity was not associated with higher risk for breast cancer diagnosed by age 50 years.

Limitations

Observational design; nonrepresentative sample limited to screening participants; and unmeasured confounding, including smoking burden.

Conclusion

Obesity in young Korean adults, measured by BMI and waist circumference, is associated with higher early-onset cancer risk persisting into midlife, with patterns varying by cancer type. Early weight management may be important for prevention.

Primary funding source

None.
title: Obesity and Cancer Risk in Young Adults in Korea : A Nationwide Health Screening Cohort Study.

authors: Booth SE, Gould R, Cibotti N, Fields R, Horng S, Jegadeesan V, Li S, Narayan D, Rubins DM, O'Donoghue AL, Simrak A, Stevens JP.
summary:
Background

Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) medical scribes may reduce documentation burden and clinician burnout. Whether use intensity drives benefits remains uncertain.

Objective

To evaluate the association between AI scribe (Heidi) enrollment and documentation burden and whether changes differ by use intensity.

Design

Retrospective quality improvement study using an interrupted time series (ITS) indexed on each clinician's enrollment month adjusted for patient demographics and visit complexity. A secondary 3-group ITS compared enrolled nonusers, low users, and high users.

Setting

14-hospital health system in Boston, Massachusetts.

Participants

902 outpatient clinicians enrolled in Heidi; 605 users and 297 enrolled nonusers.

Intervention

Heidi enrollment after system-wide implementation beginning January 2025.

Measurements

The primary outcome was note-active time. Secondary outcomes included same-day and after-hours note closures, note length, and work relative value units (wRVUs).

Results

1 637 227 encounters had notes authored by enrolled clinicians between 1 July 2024 and 31 January 2026. Enrollment was associated with an immediate reduction in note-active time (-1.21 minutes [95% CI, -1.74 to -0.68 minutes]), with larger reductions among high users (-2.50 minutes [CI, -3.55 to -1.45 minutes]) than nonusers (difference, -2.20 minutes [CI, -3.46 to -0.95 minutes]) and low users (difference, -1.72 minutes [CI, -3.03 to -0.40 minutes]). High users had greater increases in note length than nonusers (difference, +170.90 characters [CI, 21.07 to 320.70 characters]) and low users (difference, +270.70 characters [CI, 131.04 to 410.36 characters]). No differences were observed in same-day closure, after-hours closure, or wRVUs.

Limitation

Observational design with potential unmeasured confounding; inability to distinguish AI-scribed from clinician-authored notes postenrollment.

Conclusion

Heidi enrollment was associated with reductions in documentation time and increases in note length, concentrated among high users. Enrollment was not associated with improvements in same-day, after-hours note closures, or wRVUs.

Primary funding source

None.
title: Impact of Unrestricted Artificial Intelligence Scribe Deployment in a Single Health System on Clinician Workload and Productivity : A Quality Improvement Study.

authors: Ariel D, Endelman S, Laban G.
summary:
Background

The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs).

Objective

To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations.

Design

Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective.

Setting

Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026.

Participants

No human participants were involved.

Measurements

Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action).

Results

The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%).

Limitations

Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use.

Conclusion

The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations.

Primary funding source

None.
title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.

authors: Oseran AS, Liu-Hass M, Shanab BM, Zheng Z, Lalani C, Yeh RW, Wadhera RK.
summary:
Background

Medicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. Critics argue this practice increases risk-adjusted payments without improving quality. Comprehensive data on use of in-home HRAs and downstream treatment are lacking.

Objective

To examine trends in cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs, characteristics associated with HRA-based diagnoses, and treatment rates after diagnoses.

Design

Cohort study.

Setting

Population-based.

Participants

Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.

Measurements

Using 100% Medicare claims, trends in the proportion of cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs (vs. facility-based visits) were examined. Multivariable logistic regression models were fit to estimate the association between beneficiary- and plan-level characteristics and HRA-based diagnoses and compare treatment rates across settings.

Results

Among 21 496 506 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries diagnosed with a cardiovascular risk factor or disease, the proportion diagnosed during in-home HRAs increased between 2018 and 2022 for hypertension (45.9% to 47.7%), hyperlipidemia (57.8% to 66.7%), diabetes (47.8% to 51.6%), atrial fibrillation (30.0% to 36.0%), ischemic heart disease (37.2% to 41.6%), peripheral vascular disease (64.5% to 73.9%), and heart failure (34.7% to 42.6%). Racial and ethnic minority beneficiaries and those enrolled in lower-rated plans were more likely to receive HRA-based diagnoses. Treatment rates were substantially lower after HRA-based diagnoses across all conditions.

Limitations

Differences in the severity of conditions between groups could not be assessed. Prescription fills were used as a proxy for management. Observed differences in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions across encounter settings may be susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

Conclusion

Among Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, an increasingly large share of cardiovascular conditions are being diagnosed through in-home HRAs, but treatment rates after these diagnoses are consistently lower than after facility-based encounters.

Primary funding source

National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiovascular Conditions in Medicare Advantage In-Home Health Risk Assessments.

authors: Mohareb AM, Ganapathi L, Dugdale CM, Rajbhandari R, Ciaranello A, Neilan AM, Jhaveri R, Kim AY, Hyle EP.
summary:
Background

The United States recently proposed changes to the recommendations for childhood hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination.

Objective

To project the effect of vaccine policy changes, if fully implemented, on chronic HBV infections.

Design

Markov cohort state transition model of perinatal and childhood HBV infection.

Data sources

Published data on maternal HBV prevalence (0.4%) and hepatitis B surface antigen testing (99.5% sensitivity), childhood vaccine completion (universal birth-dose strategy: 91.1%; deferred strategy: 87.1%; shared decision-making strategy: 50.0%), and age-stratified risk for chronic HBV infection.

Target population

One-year birth cohort of U.S.-born infants (n = 3.6 million).

Time horizon

20 years.

Intervention

Universal birth-dose vaccination, deferred (2-month) vaccination, and vaccination through shared decision making.

Outcome measures

Numbers with chronic HBV infection and susceptibility to HBV, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) derived from probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Results of base-case analysis

Compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (255 childhood infections [95% UI, 130 to 530]), the deferred and shared decision-making strategies would increase chronic HBV infections in the 2026 birth cohort by 19% to 303 (95% UI, 155 to 610) and by 83% to 467 (95% UI, 209 to 1032), respectively. These strategies would also increase the number of HBV-susceptible people at year 20 (474 000 and 1 806 000) compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (232 000).

Results of sensitivity analysis

In a scenario with lower vaccine coverage (84.5%) and higher HBV prevalence (maternal prevalence of 0.72% and higher risk for horizontal infection), chronic HBV infections would increase to 1700 and 2192, respectively, with the deferred and shared decision-making strategies.

Limitation

Uncertainty in horizontal HBV infection risk.

Conclusion

Proposed policy changes for vaccination through shared decision making are projected to result in an 83% increase in childhood HBV infections, and between 50% and 70% of children entering adulthood annually would be susceptible to HBV infection. Policymakers should reimplement recommendations for universal birth-dose vaccination.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.
title: Projected Effect of 2026 Federal Changes to the Childhood Immunization Schedule on Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infections in the United States.

authors: Smith CC, Chelmow D, Freund KM, Burns RB.
summary: Cervical cancer is the third most common gynecologic cancer, with more than 13 000 new cases diagnosed in 2025. The incidence of and mortality from cervical cancer vary across racial and ethnic groups and in persons living in medically underserved or geographically isolated areas, with half of all cervical cancers occurring in women who are underscreened or have never been screened. Persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most important risk factor for cervical cancer and is associated with nearly all cases. Although genital tract HPV infection is common, most HPV infections are transient, and cervical cancer occurs in only a small portion of patients with HPV. For decades, cervical cancer screening relied on annual cytologic assessment. A growing understanding of the role of HPV infection in the natural progression of cervical cancer has led to updated screening recommendations from the American Cancer Society and the Women's Preventive Services Initiative, as well as a draft update from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. These recommendations include primary HPV testing as a preferred screening strategy and include an option for self-collected specimens for HPV testing. Here, 2 experts in this field, a primary care physician and an obstetrics and gynecology physician, debate how to apply these guidelines when screening a patient for cervical cancer. They discuss a range of screening options and consider the challenges of applying these guidelines across different age groups and in patients at increased risk.
title: How Would You Screen This 26-Year-Old Woman for Cervical Cancer? Grand Rounds Discussion From Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.

authors: Fung K, Sujan AC, Bateman BT, Straub L, Hernandez-Diaz S, Brill G, Zhu Y, Cohen LS, Gray KJ, Huybrechts KF.
summary:
Background

Existing data on malformations associated with benzodiazepine use in pregnancy are conflicting.

Objective

To assess the risk for major congenital malformations from first-trimester exposure to benzodiazepines.

Design

Population-based U.S. cohort study.

Setting

Medicaid (2000-2018) and Merative MarketScan (2003-2020) databases.

Participants

Pregnant persons enrolled from 90 days before pregnancy to 30 days after delivery, and their live-born infants enrolled for 90 days after birth.

Measurements

Exposure was defined as at least 1 fill of a benzodiazepine in the first trimester. Primary outcomes were any major congenital malformation and organ-specific malformations previously associated with benzodiazepine exposure. The investigators estimated relative risks (RRs) comparing exposed versus unexposed pregnancies with propensity score fine stratification weights to control for confounders. An RR of 1.3 or higher was prespecified as clinically significant.

Results

In total, 51 339 of 2 478 434 (2.1%) publicly insured and 27 779 of 1 750 721 (1.6%) commercially insured pregnancies had benzodiazepine exposure. The adjusted absolute risks for any malformation in exposed versus unexposed pregnancies were 4.0% versus 4.1% for Medicaid and 4.9% versus 4.8% for MarketScan. The pooled adjusted RR was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.96 to 1.03). Associations with organ-specific malformations were not consistently observed in sensitivity analyses, nor was a dose-response relationship observed. Analyses of different benzodiazepines yielded similar results. The risk for selected organ-specific malformations was increased in some analyses of coexposure to benzodiazepines and other psychoactive medications, but a consistent pattern did not emerge.

Limitations

Potential nondifferential exposure and outcome misclassification; analyses restricted to malformations prevalent at birth.

Conclusion

No substantial increase in the risk for malformations was consistently identified across data sources. Findings from coexposure analyses were inconsistent and warrant further study.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.
title: Benzodiazepine Use Early in Pregnancy and Risk for Congenital Malformations.

authors: Golden BP, Vasilevskis EE.
summary: Delirium is a common, acute confusional state that is associated with adverse patient, caregiver, and health system outcomes. All patients are at risk for delirium, although those with advanced age or acute infection and those taking sedatives and anticholinergics are at greater risk. The pathophysiology of delirium is complex and includes neuronal injury, inflammation, metabolic imbalance, and blood-brain barrier disruption. It is important to note that delirium is preventable; recognizing people at risk and identifying and addressing predisposing and precipitating factors is paramount. No single intervention or medication has been shown to be effective in treating delirium; therefore, standard-of-care treatments rely on multifaceted strategies to address contributing factors.
title: Delirium.

summary:
Background

Postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID) presents a therapeutic challenge, with fatigue being a common, debilitating symptom.

Objective

To assess the efficacy of fluvoxamine and metformin to treat long COVID fatigue.

Design

Randomized, placebo-controlled, adaptive trial. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06128967).

Setting

Outpatient sites in Brazil.

Participants

399 adults with fatigue 90 days to 24 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Intervention

Participants were randomly assigned to fluvoxamine (100 mg twice daily [BID]), extended-release metformin (750 mg BID [n = 71] from October 2023 to April 2024; reduced to 500 mg BID [n = 40] in May 2024 after a protocol amendment until the group was stopped for futility in September 2024), or a matching placebo, each for 60 days with follow-up to day 90.

Measurements

Change in Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) score.

Results

Median baseline FSS scores ranged from 5.6 to 5.9 across all study groups. The treatment effect on FSS score for fluvoxamine versus placebo showed a mean difference of -0.43 at day 60 and -0.58 at day 90; both had a posterior probability of superiority of 99%. Fluvoxamine also improved quality-of-life scores with a high posterior probability of superiority. Findings for metformin were inconclusive. Incidence of adverse events was lower for fluvoxamine (24.0%) than for metformin, 750 mg BID (45.1%); metformin, 500 mg BID (42.5%); and placebo (35.5%). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were rare (≤2.7%), with no treatment-related deaths.

Limitations

The results were inconclusive for metformin because of a dose change recommended by the data safety and monitoring committee due to adverse effects causing study withdrawal and early termination. The benefit of fluvoxamine after 90 days is unknown. The trial did not address other long COVID symptoms.

Conclusion

Fluvoxamine shows potential for improving long COVID-associated fatigue and quality of life.

Primary funding source

The Latona Foundation.
title: Effect of Fluvoxamine and Metformin for Fatigue in Patients With Long COVID : An Adaptive Randomized Trial.

authors: Qaseem A, Mackey K, Yost J, Shekelle PG, Shamliyan TA, Cross JT, Clinical Guidelines Committee of the American College of Physicians.
summary:
Description

The American College of Physicians (ACP) developed this clinical guideline on pharmacologic treatments for internal medicine physicians and other clinicians caring in outpatient settings for females with menopausal vasomotor symptoms.

Methods

The ACP Clinical Guidelines Committee developed this guideline based on systematic reviews on effectiveness, comparative effectiveness, harms, public and patient values and preferences, and economic evidence of pharmacologic treatments for females with menopausal vasomotor symptoms using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach.

Recommendation

In females who are seeking treatment of vasomotor symptoms.First-line treatments. ACP recommends that clinicians initiate one of the following (strong recommendation): estrogen in combination with progestogen in females with a uterus (high-certainty evidence) or estrogen monotherapy in females without a uterus (high-certainty evidence). Second-line treatments. ACP suggests that clinicians use one of the following in females who have contraindications to or do not tolerate first-line treatment (conditional recommendation): serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, either desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine (moderate-certainty evidence). Third-line treatments. ACP suggests that clinicians use one of the following in females who have contraindications to or do not tolerate first-line or second-line treatment (conditional recommendation): selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, either escitalopram or paroxetine (low-certainty evidence); the gabapentinoid gabapentin (low-certainty evidence); or neurokinin receptor antagonists, either elinzanetant or fezolinetant (moderate-certainty evidence). When selecting a treatment of vasomotor symptoms, clinicians should use an informed decision-making approach and discuss benefits, harms, contraindications, comorbid conditions, values and preferences, financial burden, and access to and availability of treatments.
title: Pharmacologic Treatments for Females With Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms: A Clinical Guideline From the American College of Physicians.
